description: Angatra are malevolent spirits of the dead in Malagasy belief: restless shades of people whose bodies were never properly buried or whose memory the living failed to preserve. They haunt tombs and places of death, feared as dangerous unlike the benevolent razana (ancestors). In some accounts neglected angatra become kinoly, murderous wraiths that roam at night.
source: Malagasy oral tradition; literature on the Malagasy ancestor cult
research_notes: Trimmed from 800+ chars; condensed spirit-of-the-dead tradition and kept the angatra-to-kinoly motif.

description: The Angelo Custode (guardian angel) is the personal angel believed to protect and guide each individual, a tenet of Catholic teaching and popular piety. Rooted in scripture (Matthew 18:10, Acts 12:15) and elaborated by Aquinas, it holds that every person receives an angel at birth. Devotion includes the 'Angel of God' prayer and the 2 October feast of the Guardian Angels.
source: Catholic devotional tradition; Roman liturgy
research_notes: Trimmed devotional filler; kept the doctrine, biblical grounding, prayer, and feast day.

description: The asema is a vampire-witch of Afro-Surinamese legend: an old man or woman by day who sheds the skin at night and flies as a blue ball of light to suck blood from sleeping victims. Householders ward it off with garlic, bitter herbs, or seeds scattered on the floor, which the asema must stop and count; it must reclaim its skin before sunrise or it is destroyed.
source: Surinamese oral tradition (Sranan); Dutch-language folklore
research_notes: Prior text wrongly placed the asema in the Baltic; it is a genuine Surinamese skin-shedding vampire. Rewritten from Surinamese tradition.

description: Bà Chúa ('Lady') is an honorific for Vietnamese female deities of trade and prosperity, above all Bà Chúa Kho ('Lady of the Storehouse') of Bắc Ninh, whose devotees borrow money from her and repay with interest, and Bà Chúa Xứ ('Lady of the Realm') of Núi Sam, Châu Đốc, honoured by a major festival in the first lunar month.
source: Vietnamese folk religion; Bà Chúa Kho and Bà Chúa Xứ cults
research_notes: Trimmed generic moralizing; anchored the generic 'Bà Chúa' entry to the documented merchant-goddess cults.

He features in winter ceremonial dances.
source: Kwakwaka'wakw oral tradition; Franz Boas ethnography

He presides over burial and the boundary between life and death; his consort is Maman Brigitte.
